Green bonds play a pivotal role in promoting sustainable development goals by channelling financial resources toward environmentally friendly projects that foster a greener, more resilient future. The analysis highlights several priorities for scaling up global financial flows aligned with the SDGs, including blended finance approaches, enhanced multilateral development bank lending, and innovative financial instruments targeting climate-development synergies.33 This study examines Nigeria's institutional arrangements for accessing and deploying climate finance effectively. Financial obligations under UNFCCC are quite critical in achieving its objectives, particularly in supporting developing countries such as Nigeria, to address climate challenges and to promote sustainable development in the country. Achieving these goals requires overcoming significant challenges related to infrastructure, finance, policy inconsistencies, and public awareness. However, seizing available opportunities for investment, technological innovation, education, and stronger policy frameworks can set Nigeria on a path toward sustainable, inclusive, and climate-resilient development. As the world collectively grapples with the impacts of climate change, the urgency to act on these sustainable development goals is greater than ever. The time to commit to sustainable solutions is now to secure a better future for generations to come. Considering the interface between climate financing and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 in Nigeria will require greater awareness and sensitisation on the importance of addressing climate change should be created by policymakers, civil society and government, as this will boost financial commitment towards climate action in Nigeria. Second is the need to strengthen partnerships with international organisations, Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs), and other countries to unlock further resources and technology transfer opportunities. Third, climate financing should be integrated into national and local development strategies, as this will ensure that climate considerations are embedded in economic planning and development agendas, thus leading to increased financing. Furthermore, strengthening of localised responses to climate change, initiatives aimed at building local capacity for climate financing and adaptation strategies, by all stakeholders, must be encouraged. Greater investment in renewable energy solutions, will lead to job creation in Nigeria, improve energy access, and reduce emissions. Finanly, there is the need to strengthen institutional capacity, through trainings and other knowledge dissemination programs to enhance the effectiveness of climate finance 675 Fasanmi & Olujobi. across all strata of the institutional mechanism and framework, to achieve a net-zero target by 2050. 676
JSON: Name: climate_finance_gap_analysis_nigeria Title: A mixed-methods doctrinal and quantitative institutional gap analysis to evaluate the effect of climate finance reforms on mobilizing funds for SDG7 and SDG13 and achieving net-zero emissions in Nigeria Short Hypothesis: Implementing coordinated institutional reforms (integrated climate finance governance), mandatory measurement-reporting-verification (MRV) systems, and a national carbon pricing mechanism will increase annual climate finance disbursements to renewable energy and adaptation projects in Nigeria by at least 30% within three years compared to the current baseline. Related Work: Existing approaches to mobilize climate finance in developing countries include public budget allocations, concessional multilateral loans and grants (e.g., global climate funds), public-private partnerships, green bonds, and carbon market instruments. Comparative studies show concessional finance and multilateral funds catalyse projects but suffer from long approval cycles and limited national absorption. PPPs and private investment can scale infrastructure but are constrained by weak regulatory certainty and perceived sovereign and project risks. Green bond and carbon market solutions improve project-specific financing but face limited market depth, high transaction costs, and weak verification in low-capacity contexts. National policy and legal reforms (e.g., climate acts) improve institutional signalling but often leave gaps in coordination, MRV capability, and enforcement, reducing fund leverage. Prior work therefore identifies recurrent weaknesses: fragmented institutions, inadequate MRV and data systems, absence of consistent carbon pricing, governance/ fiduciary risks, and insufficient private-sector enabling conditions; these limitations prevent clear causal attribution of reforms to increased disbursements. Abstract: This research designs and evaluates a mixed-methods pipeline to quantify how specific climate finance governance reforms affect mobilization of funds for SDG7 (affordable, clean energy) and SDG13 (climate action) and the trajectory to net-zero emissions in Nigeria. The approach combines doctrinal legal analysis, institutional mapping, time-series analysis of historical climate finance flows, and scenario simulation using system-dynamics and counterfactual econometric methods. The main contribution is an integrated evaluation framework that (1) identifies institutional and regulatory bottlenecks, (2) quantifies the financing uplift attributable to three reform levers—integrated institutional coordination, mandatory MRV, and carbon pricing—and (3) provides a ranked set of interventions with projected finance-disbursement and SDG indicator impacts. Expected outcomes include quantified estimates of potential annual finance increases under reform scenarios, an ablation analysis of each reform component's contribution, and a decision-ready summary for policymakers and financiers to prioritize interventions that demonstrably increase climate finance absorption and advance SDG7/13 targets toward Nigeria's net-zero objective. Experiments: Datasets: national budget allocations (2010-2025) by sector; project-level climate finance disbursements (multilateral, bilateral, private) 2010-2025; Green Climate Fund / World Bank / AfDB project databases for Nigeria; domestic green bond issuance records; electricity access and generation mix datasets; national GHG inventory and NDC submissions; MRV/verification reports where available; governance and procurement indicators; comparable data from two peer countries with reform examples (e.g., Ghana, South Africa). Baselines: (A) status quo institutional framework and historical finance flow averages; (B) cross-country peer performance. Experimental conditions/scenarios: S0 (baseline), S1 (integrated institutional coordination implemented), S2 (mandatory MRV system added to S1), S3 (carbon pricing added to S2), S4 (combined reforms plus green bond market depth expansion). Methods: (1) Interrupted time-series and difference-in-differences econometric models comparing pre/post synthetic-reform counterfactuals; (2) system-dynamics model simulating annual finance mobilization and disbursement flows under each scenario to 2030 and 2050; (3) project-level fund absorption and approval-rate analysis for proposal success; (4) stakeholder survey (N>=60) scored and analyzed quantitatively to parameterize institutional transaction costs. Evaluation metrics: annual climate finance disbursed to renewable/adaptation (USD), fund absorption rate (% projects funded vs approved), leverage ratio (private: public finance), change in electricity access rate (SDG7 indicator), annual CO2 emissions change (SDG13 proxy), proposal approval success rate, and time-to-disbursement. Ablation study: compare S3 vs S2 vs S1 to estimate marginal contribution of MRV and carbon pricing; sensitivity analysis across governance and risk parameter ranges. Validation: compare model outputs to peer-country historical outcomes and cross-validate econometric estimates against simulation results. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data availability and quality: incomplete, inconsistent, or non-disaggregated finance flow data and weak GHG inventories will limit causal inference and increase uncertainty. Attribution/confounding: concurrent macroeconomic, political, or international funding shifts may confound measured effects of the specified reforms. External validity: results calibrated to Nigeria's institutional and political economy context may not generalize to other countries. Technical model risks: system-dynamics and econometric models may be sensitive to parameter choices and face identifiability issues; simulation outcomes depend on assumed behavioral responses of private investors. Implementation realism: the hypothesis assumes timely and enforceable policy adoption, which may not occur; observed rollout delays will affect empirical tests. Governance and corruption: fiduciary weaknesses and procurement opacity may bias observed fund absorption downwards independent of reforms. Computation and scale: large temporal cross-national datasets and Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses require substantial compute resources. Measurement bias: stakeholder surveys may have selection and response biases that affect calibration of transaction-cost parameters.
